title: Should Glamsterdam's gas repricing ship as it is?
intro: Glamsterdam, Ethereum's next upgrade, raises the price of creating and reading state, so the network can safely carry far more transactions. In October 2026 the security firm ChainSecurity published findings that the new gas accounting lets the amount of gas left in a transaction go up, which some deployed contracts rely on never happening, and similar warnings had been raised on the EIP's forum thread since June. This map follows the argument, from the case for repricing to the question of whether the upgrade should ship as it is.

stops.author: Anton_ChainSecurity
stops.source_title: EIP-8037: State Creation Gas Cost Increase
stops.note: An early warning about gas checks, months before the main finding: under EIP-8037 a catch path that used to run out of gas can now complete, paid from the reservoir.

lines.text: The pattern: a contract calls a child via try/catch and, on revert, performs state changes. The catch path cannot distinguish a legitimate revert from an out-of-gas revert.
Today, forcing the catch via OOG also depletes the regular gas that the catch's SSTOREs need, so the whole tx OOGs and the state change does not persist.

Catch paths that previously did not fit within a tx (multi-SSTORE shutdown / liquidation / freeze state changes) now do, because most of their cost is paid from the reservoir rather than the inner-call gas budget.

lines.text: During these tests Chainsecurity has found a few projects that would be vulnerable after Glamsterdam since they rely on certain invariants.

Based on these findings, ACD has decided to delay the hardfork process and not fork Hoodi until the issues are resolved. During this delay, the work on Hegota is not affected and is continuing in parallel in full force.
In order to reach a pragmatic decision on the next AllCoreDev calls, we need to know what might be broken post-Glamsterdam and if there are any potential spec changes that would prevent these issues.

lines.text: Regardless of if this affects the protocols I work on or not, if breaking invariants what we’re up to, I’m out. That’s my line.

stops.author: ross.wei
stops.note: The process complaint behind the dispute: people who write contracts are not in the room when upgrades are planned.

stops.author: Ryan Berckmans
stops.note: The case for shipping: Ethereum's commitments to apps never covered opcode prices or gas introspection, and the prices were set by the people best placed to set them.

lines.text: imo ethereum's commitments to apps do not extend to gas pricing, or to total ETH fee levels, or to USD fees. And also not to opcode pricing or gas introspection that depends on those prices. We guarantee maximally credibly neutral, maximally live access to the correct state transition function.

However, pricing opcodes can't use a neutral mechanism, we need to pick magic number opcode gas prices. Some of our best people researched this extensively and picked updated magic numbers, and that's something imo we should stick with now and continue our larger plans that are on track to grow to global ubiquity.

stops.author: Giulio Rebuffo
stops.note: The limited-impact argument: the affected contracts are rare and unusual, and scaling will lower fees anyway.

lines.text: fwiw, this barely affects anyone on-chain, if you read the report from chain security, you will see that the affected contract use very esoteric mechanisms that are not present in the 99.99% of smart contracts.
also you will get more better gas costs from scaling so you wont pay more anyways.

stops.author: Ryan Berckmans
stops.note: The same day, Berckmans clarifies: he is not arguing for recklessness, and asks for more public discussion of whether gas introspection was ever a guarantee.

lines.text: I'm not advocating to push forward recklessly. That would be stupid as everybody including me is well aware that ethereum's maximal reliability is our unique value proposition.

Currently I don't think it's clear to the community whether gas introspection behavior was ever one of our guarantees. I currently don't think it ever was or is. Nor is it clear what the impact of guaranteeing it forever, or breaking it now for these contracts, would be.

stops.note: The direct rebuttal to 'gas introspection was never a guarantee': for some functions it is the only trustless tool there is.

lines.text: Gas introspection is the only way to achieve some functionality (e.g. "did this call OOG or normal revert?" or "how much should I reimburse the related?") without introducing additional trust assumptions.

lines.text: besides the already huge list of 200,000 affected contracts in ethereum/repricing-impact, i found multiple methodological issues that make it miss many more.
it affects deployment and operation of several high profile protocols, not just some random devs misusing opcodes that were given to them.

stops.author: Michael Egorov
stops.note: Michael Egorov warns that shipping as specified could force an emergency fork back, and says it can be done without breaking immutable contracts that hold funds.

lines.text:
It does look like Glamsterdam in the current form would lead to another emergency hard fork back, with a lot of drama.

I am sure, it can be made without breaking immutable contracts which hold funds

stops.author: atis elsts
stops.note: The middle position: of three options, repricing state growth is a compromise and repricing has always been part of Ethereum, but the current design has nasty flaws to fix.

lines.text: Yet, gas repricing has always been part of Ethereum. That's why Solidity's send and transfer were deprecated.

The choice is between:
1) Limiting L1 execution scaling - leaves L1 too expensive for many use cases
2) State expiry - violates CROPS, L1's core promises
3) Repricing state growth - a compromise
That said, the current design is flawed in some nasty ways.
Let's fix those problems, but let's not throw the baby out with the bathwater.

stops.author: Laurence Day
stops.affiliation: Wildcat Labs (the post says these are personal opinions, not the company's)
stops.note: A lending protocol's concrete costs: deployed, audited code repriced underneath it, Safe's execution check broken for large transactions, and the prospect of auditing twice.

lines.text: Nothing in our contracts changed: the chain reprices bytecode deposits by 7.65x underneath already-audited code.
Under EIP-8037, the GAS opcode no longer reports the reservoir, so a Safe's execution check (GS010) can never be satisfied for a transaction that needs more than the execution cap.
It is a consensus change that silently invalidates a safety check in the most widely deployed smart-contract wallet on Ethereum, with no deprecation path, and as of today nobody owns fixing it.

The cost - and the apparent lesson - of being an early, careful team on Ethereum is that you run the risk of needing to audit twice: once against the chain you deploy to, and once against the chain it becomes.

stops.author: Duncan Townsend
stops.note: A second Safe concern: Safe{Wallet} gas sponsorship needs to meter the gas a call uses, which he says EIP-8037 removes from the EVM.

lines.text: @safe's Safe{Wallet} gas sponsorship feature depends on the ability to meter the gas paid by a call. Under EIP-8037, this is no longer possible.
I don't mean that the specific implementation doesn't work correctly. I mean the entire "meter the gas consumed by a call" concept is removed from the EVM.

stops.author: kankodu
stops.note: A check on one widely cited example: the Uniswap v4 Position Manager is heavily used, but he found no immutable contract using its subscribe pattern for rewards distribution that would break.

lines.text:
Uniswap V4 Position Manager is being used as an example of highly used contract that will be broken after Glamsterdam. 

Yes, the contract itself is highly used but I couldn't find any immutable contract using the subscribe pattern in the wild for rewards distribution that will be broken. Protocols (including Uniswap Foundation) just use Merkl to provide rewards and they do calculations off-chain.

stops.author: jango.eth
stops.source_title: Post on X sharing an email to the Glamsterdam disclosure address
stops.note: Simulated findings beyond Juicebox itself: an OP Stack bridge contract on L1 that may fail to record a failed relay, and why that undermines trust in immutable protocols.

lines.text: L1CrossDomainMessenger reserves 40k gas to record a failed relay, which is less than a new slot now costs. If the target runs out of gas, the failure may go unrecorded. The portal finalizes the withdrawal with no replay, and the ETH stays in the L1 bridge.
The messenger cause is inferred from the code and the numbers, not traced.
It's impossible to trust an immutable protocol like Juicebox and Revnets if failures caused by changes to the underlying network are fair game.

stops.author: La-Li-Lu-Le-Lo
stops.note: Advice to the EF: write down what may change under deployed contracts, with app developers then carrying the risk of misreading it; give audits an expiry date by fork; and fix the final compatibility limits after Lean Ethereum.

lines.text:
My personal advice for the EF:

Create a bible of good practices in building on Ethereum and what deltas (like gas price, block time, etc.) and what behaviors (gasLeft etc.) can change and should not be relied on as core logic of non-upgradable smart contracts from now to J* / Lean Ethereum.

Also asking all auditors in the space to add a new section “Expiry Date” basically based on good practice, giving the audited code a possible vote on when the code can be broken (or not) due to not being compliant with the best practices, specified on what next fork the protocol can start to be in danger.
Then, after J* / Lean Ethereum, working on the core ossification and establishing once and for all the final limits on what can change and what MUST be always be retrocompatible.

stops.author: Ethlabs
stops.note: Ethlabs separates simple repricings, which it calls legitimate, from accounting changes that caused unforeseen problems, and recommends no decision until the audits are out. binji's post introducing it says Barnabé Monnot wrote it; the page itself is signed Ethlabs.

lines.text: It is expected that simple repricings break contracts that have hard-coded parameters.

In our view, there is no other way around these simple repricings, and they are legitimate to do as application developers were broadly expected not to condition on the fixed cost of these operations in order to derive their contract execution. This does not mean that the impacts we’ve seen so far are small, and we’ve also seen appropriate mitigations discussed with teams facing this issue.

On the other hand, beyond these simple repricings, accounting changes were also proposed as part of Glamsterdam. Some of these changes led to genuine, unforeseen problems. The task is to understand the magnitude of these issues.
Our recommendation: Do not proceed with spec changes or Hoodi scheduling until publication of findings and until findings lead to a clear position.

stops.place: Forkcast, the Ethereum Foundation blog, the EIP pages and Marius van der Wijden on X
stops.title: Hoodi postponed; both EIPs still scheduled
stops.body: Forkcast lists EIP-8037 and EIP-8038 as still Scheduled for Glamsterdam, and both EIP pages are in Last Call. Hoodi, the test network, was due to fork on 26 October, but All Core Devs Execution #248 postponed it to analyse a security disclosure affecting the repricing EIPs; Forkcast says no new date is set. The Ethereum Foundation blog of 6 November says ACD has decided to delay the hard fork process and not fork Hoodi until the issues are resolved, and that the team is working with ChainSecurity and Dedaub and asking contract developers to check their projects. On 10 November Marius van der Wijden wrote on X that there is no decision on spec changes or Hoodi yet, and that the goal is to have the audit reports before the All Core Devs Testing call on 16 November, which is set for findings and an open Q&A, with app developers welcome. The proposed fix, EIPs#12581, is still open and no call has agreed it. The Ethlabs page of 10 November says the All Core Devs Consensus call on 12 November is expected to give only a minimal update, and the Ethereum Foundation blog says the Dedaub and ChainSecurity engagements end on 13 November. The next All Core Devs Execution call, #249, is on 19 November 2026.
